subject: math
title: Grade 3 Bar Graphs and Pictographs
seo_title: Grade 3 Bar Graphs and Pictographs Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: One-to-one correspondence with bar graphs, pictographs, charts, and tables
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on bar graphs and pictographs for the BC curriculum: tally charts and tables, pictographs where 1 symbol = 1, bar graphs with a scale of 1 or 2, comparing and totalling data, and drawing conclusions. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: One symbol or one tally mark stands for one thing. Count carefully, then read across to the right number.
key_sub: A group of tally marks is 5, not 4. Keep your finger on the right bar or row. If the scale counts by 2s, a bar halfway between 8 and 10 shows 9.
body_html:
Collect, count, show, then explain

Data is information we collect, such as votes in a class survey. First we ask a clear question. Then we count the answers with tally marks. Then we show them in a table, a pictograph or a bar graph. Last, we say what the data tells us.

Tally charts and tables

Draw one mark for each answer. The fifth mark goes across the other four. Count the groups by 5s, then count on the single marks.

Pictographs: 1 symbol = 1

Look at the key first. In Grade 3, one symbol stands for one thing. This is called one-to-one correspondence. Count the symbols in a row to find the number.

Example

How many more students chose soccer than hockey?

Soccer has 8 circles. Hockey has 5. 8 − 5 = 3. You can also count the 3 extra circles in the Soccer row.

Answer: 3 more students

Bar graphs

A good bar graph has a title, labels, a scale and a source (where the data came from). Find what the scale counts by: 1s or 2s. Put your finger on the top of the bar and look straight across to the scale. If the scale counts by 2s and a bar ends halfway between two lines, the number is halfway between them.

Example

How many more rainy days were there in November than in December?

November ends on 20. December is halfway between 18 and 20, so 19. 20 − 19 = 1.

Answer: 1 more rainy day

Ask questions and draw conclusions

A good survey question has a few clear choices, and each person picks one. After you make the graph, compare the bars or rows: which is the most, which is the least, and how many more? Only say what the data shows. A vote in one class tells us about that class, not about everyone.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting a group of 5 tally marks as 4Count the line across too: each group is 5
Counting each group of tally marks as 1Count the groups by 5s: 5, 10, 15
Reading the wrong bar or rowKeep your finger on the right bar, then look across
Counting one symbol too many or too fewTouch each symbol as you count
Counting grid spaces when the scale counts by 2sRead the number on the scale
Adding when the question asks how many moreHow many more means subtract

faq.q: What do Grade 3 students learn about graphs in the BC math curriculum?
faq.a: The BC Grade 3 curriculum includes one-to-one correspondence with bar graphs, pictographs, charts and tables. Students collect data, count it with tally marks, show it so that one symbol or one square stands for one thing, and talk about what the data shows.

faq.q: What is one-to-one correspondence in a pictograph?
faq.a: It means each symbol stands for exactly one thing. If the key says 1 star = 1 student, then a row of 6 stars shows 6 students. In Grade 4, students move on to keys where 1 symbol stands for 2, 5 or 10.

faq.q: How do you count tally marks?
faq.a: Each group of five tally marks has four lines and one line across. Count the groups by 5s, then count on the single marks: 2 groups and 3 marks is 5, 10, then 11, 12, 13.

faq.q: How can I help my child read a bar graph?
faq.a: Ask them to read the title and labels first, then check what the scale counts by. Have them put a finger on the top of one bar and look straight across to the scale, so they read the right bar.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups by 5s, then count on the single marks. 1 group of 5, then 2 more: 5, then 6, 7. So 7. (6 counts each group as 4. Count the line across too.)

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups by 5s, then count on the single marks. 2 groups of 5, then 2 more: 5, 10, then 11, 12. So 12. (10 counts each group as 4. Count the line across too.)

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups by 5s, then count on the single marks. 1 group of 5, then 4 more: 5, then 6, 7, 8, 9. So 9. (8 counts each group as 4. Count the line across too.)

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups by 5s, then count on the single marks. 3 groups of 5, then 1 more: 5, 10, 15, then 16. So 16. (13 counts each group as 4. Count the line across too.)
13 = 5 + 5 + 3, so look for 2 groups of 5 and 3 single marks. That is C. A shows 12 (one mark too few), B shows 18 (one group of 5 too many) and D shows 14 (one mark too many).

items.q: What number should go in the Total column for Soccer?
items.e: Soccer has 2 groups of 5, then 1 more: 5, 10, then 11. So 11. (9 counts the group of 5 as 4 marks.)

items.q: How many students chose hockey?
items.e: Find the Hockey row. The tally shows 1 group of 5, then 3 more: 5, then 6, 7, 8. So 8. Do not read the Lacrosse row below it (4).

items.q: Which sport did the fewest students choose?
items.e: Lacrosse has only 4 single marks. Every other sport has at least one group of 5.

items.q: How many more students chose hockey than swimming?
items.e: Hockey 8, swimming 7. How many more means find the difference: 8 − 7 = 1. (15 adds them instead.)

items.q: Every student voted once. How many students voted?
items.e: Soccer 11, hockey 8, lacrosse 4, swimming 7, basketball 6. 11 + 8 + 4 + 7 + 6 = 36. (25 leaves out soccer, the row with the ?. 31 counts each group of 5 as 4.)

items.q: How many days in October were cloudy?
items.e: Find the Cloudy row, then read across to the Days column: 9. (15 is the Rainy row above it, and 5 is the Sunny row below it.)

items.q: How many more rainy days than sunny days were there?
items.e: Rainy 15, sunny 5. 15 − 5 = 10 more rainy days. (20 adds instead of subtracting; 6 uses the Cloudy row by mistake: 15 − 9.)

items.q: October has 31 days. How many days were not rainy?
items.e: 31 − 15 = 16. Check: cloudy, sunny and foggy are 9 + 5 + 2 = 16. (15 is the number of rainy days.)

items.q: Which kind of day happened most often?
items.e: Rainy has the biggest number in the table: 15 days. That is almost half of October.

items.q: How many juncos came to the feeder?
items.e: The Junco row has 2 groups of 5: 5, 10. So 10. (8 counts each group as 4 marks; 9 is the Sparrow row below it.)

items.q: Which bird came 14 times?
items.e: 14 = 5 + 5 + 4. The Chickadee row has 2 groups of 5 and 4 single marks.

items.q: Leah counts 8 votes for hockey. Which tally is right?
items.e: 8 = 5 + 3. Draw 1 group of 5 (four lines and one line across) and 3 single marks.

items.q: Noah makes a tally of the cars that go past the school. He draws 3 groups of 5 and 2 single marks. How many cars went past?
items.e: Count the groups by 5s: 5, 10, 15. Then count on 2: 16, 17. So 17 cars. (14 counts each group as 4. 5 counts each group as 1.)

items.q: Sofia counted 19 votes for blueberries. How should she draw the tally?
items.e: 19 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 4. Draw 3 groups of 5 and 4 single marks. Never leave 5 or more single marks: make another group of 5.

items.q: Ji-woo’s tally chart shows 2 groups of 5 for orcas and 1 group of 5 and 4 marks for seals on a whale-watching trip near Victoria. How many more orcas than seals did the class see?
items.e: Orcas: 5, 10, so 10. Seals: 5, then 6, 7, 8, 9, so 9. 10 − 9 = 1 more orca. (19 adds them. 5 more compares only the groups.)

items.q: Look at the key. What does one circle stand for?
items.e: The key is under the pictograph. It says one circle = 1 student. So we count the circles one by one.
Count the stars in the Chinook row: 9 stars. Each star stands for 1, so the row shows 9. (8 is the Chum row next to it. Keep your finger on the right row.)

items.q: How many students chose hockey?
items.e: Count the squares in the Hockey row: 7 squares. Each square stands for 1, so the row shows 7. (9 is the Soccer row next to it. Keep your finger on the right row.)

items.q: Which row shows the most books?
items.e: Every circle stands for 1, so the longest row shows the most. Count the circles in the Arjun row: 7 circles. Each circle stands for 1, so the row shows 7.
Count the stars in the Cherry row: 2 stars. Each star stands for 1, so the row shows 2. (8 is the Apple row next to it. Keep your finger on the right row.)

items.q: Which row shows 9 laps?
items.e: Count the squares in each row. Count the squares in the Leah row: 9 squares. Each square stands for 1, so the row shows 9.

items.q: Which row shows the fewest birds?
items.e: Every circle stands for 1, so the shortest row shows the fewest. Count the circles in the Heron row: 2 circles. Each circle stands for 1, so the row shows 2.
Count the stars in the Car row: 9 stars. Each star stands for 1, so the row shows 9. (5 is the Bike row next to it. Keep your finger on the right row.)

items.q: Which row shows 5 salmon?
items.e: Count the squares in each row. Count the squares in the Chum row: 5 squares. Each square stands for 1, so the row shows 5.

items.q: How many more students chose basketball than lacrosse?
items.e: Each circle stands for 1 student. Basketball: 5. Lacrosse: 3. How many more means find the difference: 5 − 3 = 2. You can also count the extra circles at the end of the Basketball row. (8 adds instead of subtracting.)
Count the stars in the Blueberry row: 8 stars. Each star stands for 1, so the row shows 8. (4 is the Pear row next to it. Keep your finger on the right row.)

items.q: How many fewer laps did Zara run than Owen?
items.e: Each square stands for 1 lap. Zara: 3. Owen: 6. How many fewer means find the difference: 6 − 3 = 3. (9 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: How many more bald eagles than crows were seen?
items.e: Each circle stands for 1 bird. Eagle: 4. Crow: 1. How many more means find the difference: 4 − 1 = 3. You can also count the extra circles at the end of the Eagle row. (5 adds instead of subtracting.)
Each star stands for 1 book. Olivia: 7. Arjun: 1. Altogether means add: 7 + 1 = 8.

items.q: How many rows show more than 4 students?
items.e: Read every row: Bike 1, Bus 3, Car 7, Walk 4. More than 4 means 4 itself does not count. Rows with more than 4: Car. That is 1 row.

items.q: Ava makes a pictograph of the books she read. The key says one star = 1 book. Ava read 7 books. How many stars should she draw in her row?
items.e: One star stands for 1 book, so draw one star for each book: 7 books, 7 stars. Count them as you draw so you do not draw one too many or one too few.
The Olivia row has 2 stars. 2 more is 2 + 2 = 4. The Ethan row has 4.

items.q: How many students voted altogether?
items.e: Each square stands for 1 student. Read every row: Peach 2, Apple 3, Blueberry 7, Cherry 9. Add them: 2 + 3 + 7 + 9 = 21. (12 leaves out the last row.)

items.q: The Heron row is not drawn yet. Altogether there are 29 birds. How many birds should the Heron row show?
items.e: Add the rows you can see: 2 + 9 + 5 + 7 = 23. Then 29 − 23 = 6. So draw 6 circles.

Each star stands for 1 salmon. Chinook: 7. Pink: 5. How many more means find the difference: 7 − 5 = 2. You can also count the extra stars at the end of the Chinook row. (12 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 1, 2, 3 … Each line is 1 more than the one below it, so the scale counts by 1s.

items.q: How many students chose lacrosse?
items.e: The scale goes up by 1s. The bar for Lacrosse ends on the line for 3. (2 is the Hockey bar next to it. Look straight across from the top of the right bar.)

items.q: Which bar shows 9 laps?
items.e: The scale goes up by 1s. Find 9 on the scale and look across. The bar for Zara ends on the line for 9.

items.q: How many ducks were seen?
items.e: The scale goes up by 1s. The bar for Duck ends on the line for 10. (8 is the Heron bar next to it. Look straight across from the top of the right bar.)

items.q: Which bar shows the most salmon?
items.e: The bar for Chum is the tallest one. The bar for Chum ends on the line for 9.

items.q: Which bar shows the fewest students?
items.e: The bar for Bus is the shortest one. The bar for Bus ends on the line for 2.

items.q: How many students chose basketball?
items.e: The scale goes up by 1s. The bar for Basketball ends on the line for 5. (9 is the Soccer bar next to it. Look straight across from the top of the right bar.)

items.q: Which bar shows 9 books?
items.e: The scale goes up by 1s. Find 9 on the scale and look across. The bar for Simran ends on the line for 9.

items.q: Which list matches this bar graph? The numbers are in this order: Cherry, Peach, Apple, Blueberry.
items.e: The scale goes up by 1s. The bar for Cherry ends on the line for 1. The bar for Peach ends on the line for 5. The bar for Apple ends on the line for 9. The bar for Blueberry ends on the line for 8. (5, 1, 9, 8 swaps the first two bars.)

items.q: Laps at the Terry Fox Run: Kai 6, Leah 9, Owen 4, Zara 7. Which bar graph shows this data?
items.e: B matches every number (the lines go up by 1s, with a number on every second line). A: two bars are the wrong way round; C: one bar is one line too high; D: one bar is one line too low.

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 2, 4, 6 … Each line is 2 more than the one below it, so the scale counts by 2s. (Do not count the lines by 1s.)

items.q: How many rainy days were there in January?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Jan ends on the line for 14. (7 counts the grid spaces, and 19 is the Dec bar next to it.)

items.q: How many cans did Mr. Chen’s class collect?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Mr. Chen ends halfway between 12 and 14, so it shows 13. (12 and 14 are the lines below and above it.)

items.q: Which bar shows 20 rainy days?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Find 20 on the scale and look across. The bar for Dec ends on the line for 20.

items.q: How many cans did Mr. Gill’s class collect?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Mr. Gill ends halfway between 14 and 16, so it shows 15. (14 and 16 are the lines below and above it.)

items.q: Which bar shows the most rainy days?
items.e: The bar for Jan is the tallest one. The bar for Jan ends on the line for 20.

items.q: How many cans did Ms. Lee’s class collect?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Ms. Lee ends on the line for 10. (5 counts the grid spaces, and 12 is the Ms. Ward bar next to it.)

items.q: Which bar shows 15 rainy days?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Find 15 on the scale and look across. The bar for Oct ends halfway between 14 and 16, so it shows 15.

items.q: Which list matches this bar graph? The numbers are in this order: Heron, Duck, Eagle, Gull, Crow.
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Heron ends on the line for 12. The bar for Duck ends on the line for 14. The bar for Eagle ends on the line for 8. The bar for Gull ends halfway between 14 and 16, so it shows 15. The bar for Crow ends halfway between 10 and 12, so it shows 11. (12, 14, 8, 14, 10 reads the bars between two lines as the line below, and 12, 14, 8, 16, 12 as the line above.)

items.q: Birds seen in Stanley Park: Crow 12, Duck 7, Gull 16, Owl 10. Which bar graph shows this data?
items.e: D matches every number (the scale goes up by 2s). A: two bars are the wrong way round; B: a bar is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); C: one bar is one line too high.

items.q: How many more laps did Owen run than Ryan?
items.e: Owen: 7. Ryan: 5. How many more means find the difference: 7 − 5 = 2. (12 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: How many fewer students chose soccer than basketball?
items.e: Basketball: 4. Soccer: 2. How many fewer means find the difference: 4 − 2 = 2. (6 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: How many students chose blueberries or apples?
items.e: Blueberry: 5. Apple: 8. Altogether means add: 5 + 8 = 13.

items.q: How many students are in the survey altogether?
items.e: Read every row: Car: 9, Walk: 7, Bike: 8, Bus: 3. Add them all: 9 + 7 + 8 + 3 = 27. Make sure you add every row once.

items.q: How many more books did Olivia read than Ethan?
items.e: Olivia: 13. Ethan: 4. How many more means find the difference: 13 − 4 = 9. (17 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: How many more sockeye salmon than pink salmon were seen?
items.e: Sockeye: 10. Pink: 1. How many more means find the difference: 10 − 1 = 9. (11 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: How many students walk or take the bus to school?
items.e: Walk: 3. Bus: 9. Altogether means add: 3 + 9 = 12.

items.q: How many fewer rainy days were there in January than in October?
items.e: Oct: 14. Jan: 11. How many fewer means find the difference: 14 − 11 = 3. (25 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: How many more salmon does the tallest bar show than the shortest bar?
items.e: The tallest bar is Coho (7). The shortest is Sockeye (1). 7 − 1 = 6.

items.q: How many birds are not in the Crow row?
items.e: Total: 9 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 22. Take away Crow (4): 22 − 4 = 18. You can also add the other rows: 9 + 8 + 1 = 18.

items.q: How many cans did Mr. Chen’s class and Mr. Gill’s class collect altogether?
items.e: Mr. Chen: 14. Mr. Gill: 19. Altogether means add: 14 + 19 = 33.

items.q: How many students voted altogether?
items.e: Read every bar: Swimming: 4, Soccer: 6, Lacrosse: 2, Hockey: 5. Add them all: 4 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17. Make sure you add every bar once.

items.q: How many more laps does Zara need to catch up to Leah?
items.e: Leah: 7. Zara: 4. Count up from 4 to 7: that is 7 − 4 = 3 more. (7 is Leah’s number, not how many more.)

items.q: How many more rainy days were there in January than in November?
items.e: Jan: 20. Nov: 12. How many more means find the difference: 20 − 12 = 8. (32 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: How many books are not in the Mei bar?
items.e: Total: 8 + 3 + 4 + 9 + 2 = 26. Take away Mei (4): 26 − 4 = 22. You can also add the other bars: 8 + 3 + 9 + 2 = 22.

items.q: How many fewer students chose cherries than peaches?
items.e: Peach: 7. Cherry: 3. How many fewer means find the difference: 7 − 3 = 4. (10 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q: How many more cans does the tallest bar show than the shortest bar?
items.e: The tallest bar is Ms. Ward (20). The shortest is Ms. Lee (6). 20 − 6 = 14.

items.q: How many more books does Ethan need to catch up to Simran?
items.e: Simran: 10. Ethan: 3. Count up from 3 to 10: that is 10 − 3 = 7 more. (10 is Simran’s number, not how many more.)

items.q: How many rainy days were there altogether?
items.e: Read every bar: Oct: 20, Nov: 18, Dec: 11, Jan: 12, Feb: 14. Add them all: 20 + 18 + 11 + 12 + 14 = 75. Make sure you add every bar once.
Step 1: Hockey and Basketball together: 2 + 3 = 5. Step 2: Swimming: 8. 8 − 5 = 3.

items.q: Which question did the class ask to get this data?
c: What will you do over Spring Break?
How many days is Spring Break?
items.e: The bars are camping, skiing, beach and visit family. These are answers to “What will you do over Spring Break?” “Do you like skiing?” only has yes or no answers.

items.q: How many students are in the survey?
items.e: Skiing ends halfway between 10 and 12, so 11. Visit family ends halfway between 8 and 10, so 9. 6 + 11 + 4 + 9 = 30. (28 reads 11 and 9 as 10 and 8. 15 counts the grid spaces.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: Camping and skiing are the same.
More students will ski than camp.
Fewer students will visit family than go to the beach.
The beach is the most popular plan.
items.e: Skiing 11 and camping 6, so more students will ski. The beach (4) is the least popular, and visit family (9) is more than the beach (4).

items.q: Zara says, “Half of the class will go skiing.” Is she right?
c: No. 11 is less than half of 30.
Yes. Skiing has the tallest bar.
items.e: There are 30 students, and half of 30 is 15. Only 11 will ski. The tallest bar shows the most popular plan, not half of the class.

items.q: What can the class say from this pictograph?
c: Car and bike are the same.
Walking is the most common way.
items.e: The Walk row is the longest: 8 circles. The Bus row is the shortest (3), and 5 students bike.

items.q: The school wants fewer cars at drop-off. If 2 of the car students start to bike, how many students will bike?
items.e: Bike now: 5. 2 more will bike: 5 + 2 = 7. (4 is the new number of car students: 6 − 2.)

items.q: Which question can you not answer with this pictograph?
c: How many students walk to school?
How far away does each student live?
How many students were in the survey?
Do more students bike or take the bus?
items.e: The pictograph shows how students get to school, not how far they live. We can read the walkers (8), compare bike and bus (5 and 3), and add for the total (22).

items.q: Liam wants to make a bar graph of his class’s favourite fruit. Which survey question is best?
c: Which fruit do you like best: apple, cherry, peach or pear?
How many apples are in BC?
items.e: A good survey question gives a few clear choices, and each student picks one. Then every answer fits one bar. “Do you like fruit?” only gives yes or no.

items.q: Mei asks, “Which do you like best: soccer, hockey or lacrosse?” Kai likes basketball best. What should Mei add to her choices?
items.e: Adding “Other” gives every student an answer to pick. Each student still votes only once.

items.q: Which month had the most rainy days?
items.e: The tallest bar is November. It ends on the line for 20.

items.q: How many more rainy days were there in November than in October?
items.e: November ends on 20. October ends halfway between 14 and 16, so 15. 20 − 15 = 5. (Reading October as 14 gives 6; as 16 gives 4.)

items.q: November has 30 days. How many November days were not rainy?
items.e: Rainy days in November: 20. 30 − 20 = 10 days were not rainy. (12 uses December’s bar, 18.)

items.q: Owen says, “It rains every day in Vancouver.” Does the graph agree?
c: No. Every month had some days with no rain.
No. It never rains in January.
Yes. All the bars are tall.
items.e: Every month has 30 or 31 days, and no bar reaches 30. So each month had some dry days. The bars are tall, so it rains a lot, but not every day.

items.q: Division 3 says, “We ran the most laps.” How many more laps is that than Division 2?
items.e: Division 3: 50. Division 2: 35. 50 − 35 = 15. (8 uses Division 1: 50 − 42. 12 uses Division 4: 50 − 38.)

items.q: The school’s goal is 160 laps. Did the four divisions reach it?
items.e: 42 + 35 + 50 + 38 = 165. 165 is more than 160, so they reached the goal. (50 is only the biggest number in the table.)
Coho: 7 + 2 = 9. Pink: 9. Now coho and pink are the same, so it is a tie.
Chinook 3, coho 7, chum 5, pink 9. 3 + 7 + 5 + 9 = 24. (4 is the number of rows; 15 leaves out pink.)

items.q: Ms. Ward’s class wants to catch up to Mr. Gill’s class. How many more cans does it need?
items.e: Mr. Gill: 18. Ms. Ward: halfway between 8 and 10, so 9. 18 − 9 = 9 more cans. (Reading Ms. Ward’s bar as 8 or 10 gives 10 or 8.)

items.q: Which two classes together collected 26 cans?
items.e: Ms. Lee 14 and Mr. Chen 12: 14 + 12 = 26. (Mr. Gill and Ms. Ward: 18 + 9 = 27. Ms. Lee and Mr. Gill: 32. Ms. Ward and Mr. Chen: 21.)

items.q: Harjot says, “Mr. Gill’s class collected twice as many cans as Ms. Ward’s class.” Is he right?
c: Yes. Mr. Gill has the shortest bar.
No. Ms. Lee collected the most.
items.e: Mr. Gill 18, Ms. Ward 9. Double 9 is 9 + 9 = 18, so Harjot is right. Mr. Gill has the tallest bar.
